title: Analysis of LP relaxations for multiway and multicut problems
contribution: Derives known and new LP relaxations of multiway cut from one exact nonlinear formulation, strengthens them through a stable-set reformulation with perfect-graph integrality cases, and bounds their gap by 2(1 − 1/k) with a single-threshold randomized rounding (4/3 for k = 4; 2α(H)(1 − 1/|V(H)|) for multicut).
problem_entry: {IO+LO} Multiway cut is NP-hard for k ≥ 3, and Chopra–Owen's extended formulation was supported only by computational results; entry: bound analytically how far such relaxations can lie from the integer optimum (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: An exact nonlinear formulation with linear constraints, whose continuous relaxation is already exact (Theorem 1, p. 3), generates EF1 (Chopra–Owen), EF2 and a new convex EF3 by linearization (pp. 3–5); a stable-set map gives the stronger IND (pp. 7–10); one shared uniform threshold rounds EF3 within 2(1 − 1/k) (Theorem 11, p. 11).
assumptions: Graph with nonnegative edge weights (needed for EF1 = EF2 = EF3, p. 4) and k terminals; multicut adds a demand graph H with independence number α(H) (p. 12); no data.
proof_devices: exactness of the continuous relaxation by random assignment with probabilities ȳ_j(u) (Theorem 1, p. 3)
single shared uniform threshold: P{(u,v) cut} = |ȳ_j(u) − ȳ_j(v)|, matched to EF3's constraint (Theorem 11, p. 11); derandomized by conditioning (p. 11)
integrality-gap lower bounds: Cunningham's 16/15 example and an asymptotic 10/9 family (pp. 6–7)
perfect graphs and clique-gluing for integrality on trees and triangular cacti (Theorems 7–10, pp. 9–10)
polynomial separation of the clique constraints of I(G) (Theorem 6, p. 9)
positioning: Restates Dalhaus et al.'s 2(1 − 1/k) combinatorial bound against the LP value instead of the integer optimum (p. 11) and derives the Chopra–Owen, path and tree formulations (Chopra–Rao, Cunningham) as special cases (pp. 3–6).
writing: Contributions listed section by section (p. 2); a footnote concedes that one corollary may already be known (p. 8).
limits_future: Open: the gap between the upper bound 2 and the 10/9 example, and whether IND improves the bound (p. 13).

method_links.note: IO form of formulation-first: one exact formulation generates the rival family's relaxations, and the paper prints where its analysis stops (2 against 10/9); the class kept is an LP relaxation, not a robust or learned model

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: probabilistic reading of a relaxation solution
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: LP values read as assignment probabilities, both to prove the nonlinear relaxation exact and to round EF3 with one shared threshold
the LP relaxation is the object of study; Dalhaus et al.'s combinatorial algorithm becomes an LP relaxation with the same worst-case bound (4/3 for k = 4; the multicut factor)

transferable: Bound an integrality gap with a rounding whose per-edge cut probability equals the term the relaxation constrains (|ȳ_j(u) − ȳ_j(v)| ≤ 2x(u,v)), so the factor follows line by line (pp. 4, 11).
Write one exact nonlinear model with linear constraints; each valid linearization of its products is then a relaxation, and comparing formulations becomes algebra (pp. 3–5).
Pair the upper bound on a gap with an explicit instance family forcing a lower bound, and state the remaining interval as open (pp. 6–7, 13).

quotes.text: We also introduce a new randomized rounding argument to study the sharpness of these formulations.
However, our result is a little stronger in that the bound on the heuristic solution is in terms of the linear programming relaxation and not the optimal integer solution.

title: Bounds and policies for dynamic routing in loss networks
contribution: Builds first-, second- and third-order LP relaxations of the loss-network admission and routing MDP from balance equations of aggregated chains, giving upper bounds equal to or slightly tighter than Kelly's, and reads dynamic and static routing policies off the third-order relaxation that match or beat DAR within 0–10% of the bound.
problem_entry: {SD+LO} Blocking probabilities are #P-complete even for a fixed policy, the existing bounds (max-flow, Kelly 1994) give no policies, and practice runs DAR; entry: derive bounds and policies from the same relaxations (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: Variables are stationary probabilities of partial states (x = P{state, accept}, y = P{state}); balance equations of aggregated chains give LPs containing the achievable region, ordered by interaction (Theorems 3–5, pp. 4–8); policies accept with x/y (dynamic) or with marginals (static) (pp. 10–11).
assumptions: Complete graph, alternative routes with one intermediate node, Poisson arrivals, exponential holding times with a common rate, Markovian policies in steady state (p. 2); μ = 1 and C_ij = 10 in the experiments (pp. 12–13).
proof_devices: probability-flow balance equations of aggregated MDPs as LP constraints (Theorems 1, 3–5, pp. 3–8)
single-link ladder: max-flow O(1), relaxation O(C), Miller's exact LP O(C²); only the relaxation yields a policy (pp. 3–4)
variable counts per relaxation order: O(NRC), 3NC² + NR, 2NRC² (pp. 5, 6, 8)
symmetric reduction to O(1), O(C), O(C²) LPs (pp. 8–9)
experiments: CPLEX bounds (no version) and simulated policies with standard deviations on five-node symmetric and asymmetric networks plus one larger network (Tables I–VIII, pp. 6–14); best bound/best policy 0–2.5% under symmetric and 4–10% under asymmetric rewards (p. 13); the static policy is best in 27 of 34 instance columns, DAR in 3 (pp. 6–13); in four asymmetric-capacity columns of Tables IV–V the second-order bound lies below the third-order one (pp. 10, 12), although the text calls (9) the tightest (p. 13).
positioning: Generalizes Bertsimas–Paschalidis–Tsitsiklis 1994 to loss networks (p. 2); presents the second-order relaxation as close in spirit to Kelly's DP bound (p. 8); the baseline DAR is the practice heuristic (pp. 1–2, 12).
writing: Contributions as a two-item list (p. 2); a numbered list of qualitative insights explains why the policies succeed (p. 14).
limits_future: Bounds only slightly stronger than Kelly's (p. 15); trunk reservation needs rethinking for asymmetric rewards (p. 12); more realistic settings left as a necessary continuation (p. 15).

method_links.note: SD control problem rewritten as LPs over performance vectors that contain the achievable region, with variable counts printed per level (SW1 programme)
duel against the practice heuristic (DAR; LBA) with a per-instance gap from the bound (best bound/best policy), but by simulation and without an exact solve

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: first-, second- and third-order aggregations of the routing MDP with growing variable counts; enlarging the aggregated state further would recover the exact MDP

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: policy from the relaxation, certified by the same relaxation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: dynamic and static policies read off the third-order LP as conditional or marginal acceptance probabilities; suboptimality reported as best bound/best policy

transferable: Build a ladder of LP relaxations by aggregating an intractable MDP to partial state descriptions of growing order, writing only balance, capacity and offered-traffic constraints, and tabulate the variables per rung (pp. 3–8).
Read a randomized policy off a relaxation as conditional probabilities x/y; when two marginal estimates disagree, test simple combinations (min, average) empirically (p. 10).
Report suboptimality as best bound / best policy so that each instance carries its own gap (p. 13).

quotes.text: To the best of our knowledge, there is no systematic approach to derive policies from relaxations.
The suboptimality guarantees defined as best bound/best policy range from 0 to 2.5% under symmetry conditions

title: Performance of multiclass Markovian queueing networks via piecewise linear Lyapunov functions
contribution: Turns linear and piecewise linear Lyapunov functions from stability analysis into explicit geometric upper and lower bounds on steady-state queue-length tails of multiclass Markovian networks, including E L = O(1/(1 − ρ*)²) for two-station reentrant lines and for feedforward networks.
problem_entry: {SD+LO} Performance analysis of multiclass networks is open and at least as hard as stability; quadratic-Lyapunov LP bounds are numerical, expectation-only and can be inconclusive; entry: turn stability tools into performance tools (pp. 2–4).
key_idea: A Lyapunov function with drift γ, exception level B and bounded jumps yields geometric tail and expectation bounds (Theorem 1, pp. 8–11); linear lower Lyapunov functions give closed-form lower bounds, including for virtual stations (pp. 11–16); smoothed feasible solutions of the Down–Meyn and Dai–Vande Vate LPs give upper bounds, O(1/(1 − ρ*)²) for two stations (pp. 19–25).
assumptions: Poisson arrivals, exponential services, deterministic routing, infinite buffers, no reneging (pp. 4–5); Markovian preemptive policies only, FIFO excluded (p. 5); stability assumed a priori (p. 7).
proof_devices: tail recursion from the stationarity identity applied to max(c, Φ) (Lemma 1, pp. 9, 29)
linear lower Lyapunov functions with tail-sum load coefficients and drift parameter 1 − ρ_σj (Proposition 2, p. 12)
uniform random perturbation of LP coefficients to smooth a max of linear functions, with an explicit exception constant (Proposition 7, pp. 20–21)
LP slack ε ≥ 1 − ρ* turned into a drift bound (Lemma 2, Theorem 5, pp. 23–25)
experiments: none (worked examples: the Lu–Kumar network and a 3-station, 6-class reentrant line, pp. 17–19, 27–28)
positioning: Claims the first explicit geometric tail bounds at this generality, against numerical expectation bounds from quadratic Lyapunov functions (pp. 1, 4, 29); re-establishes Down–Meyn with explicit constants (p. 20); improves O(1/(1 − ρ*)^{J0}) for feedforward networks (p. 27).
writing: Contributions as a numbered list in §1.1 (pp. 3–4); points to a heavy-traffic singularity at ρ2 + ρ4 + ρ6 = 2 as not observed before (p. 19).
limits_future: Upper bounds are numerical except for two-station reentrant lines (p. 3); whether finiteness matches fluid global stability for the stochastic network remains to be seen (p. 29); removing the exponent 2 is left open (p. 29).

method_links.note: an LP (the stability LP) is the device, and its feasible solution certifies a probabilistic performance bound rather than an optimal policy

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: stability certificate reused as a performance bound
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: any feasible solution of the stability LP, once smoothed, becomes a Lyapunov function whose drift yields explicit tail bounds; for two stations the bounds are finite exactly when the fluid network is globally stable

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: print the looseness of your own constants and the conjecture that would close it
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the conclusion asks for removing the exponent 2 and leaves open whether finiteness matches fluid stability for stochastic networks

transferable: Apply a stability Lyapunov function's drift inequality to max(c, Φ) under the stationary law to get a geometric recursion for P(Φ > B + 2ν_max m); a lower Lyapunov function gives lower bounds by the same template (pp. 8–11).
Smooth a piecewise linear Lyapunov function by averaging over uniform perturbations of its LP coefficients, and carry the box sizes into an explicit exception constant (pp. 20–21).
For lower bounds use linear functions with tail-sum load coefficients, so that only arrivals raise the function and the drift parameter is 1 − ρ_σj (p. 12).

quotes.text: The goal of this paper is to turn some of the stability analysis tools into useful performance analysis tools.
It would be interesting to strengthen this result, perhaps by removing the exponent 2.

title: From fluid relaxations to practical algorithms for job shop scheduling: the makespan objective
contribution: Rounds the closed-form fluid relaxation of high-multiplicity job-shop makespan with a fair-queueing rule (FSA), proving an additive error of at most (I + 2)Pmax Jmax and hence asymptotic optimality, and shows on OR-library benchmarks that it beats dispatch rules from N = 10 on and scales where the shifting bottleneck heuristic does not.
problem_entry: {SD+IO} J||Cmax is NP-hard and approximation schemes are impractical; entry: the high-multiplicity regime, where a fluid relaxation from multiclass queueing control is solvable in closed form (pp. 2, 5, 7–9).
key_idea: Combine the fluid relaxation (processor-sharing-like optimal rates giving Cmax) with fair queueing based on start times: schedule the available job with the smallest nominal start time, the fluid start time corrected for discrete precedence (pp. 2, 7–11, 17); Theorem 4 gives Cmax ≤ C* ≤ C_D ≤ Cmax + max_i Σ_l (2P + U) (pp. 26–27).
assumptions: Integer processing times, non-preemptive schedules, one task per machine at a time, ordered stages (pp. 2, 5); fixed numbers of job types and stages with growing multiplicity (p. 3); deterministic arrivals in §3 (p. 28).
proof_devices: congestion lower bound and closed-form fluid optimum (Propositions 1–2, pp. 6–8)
potential φ_r(t) = max{T^c − T^d, −p_r} charging lag and crediting at most one job of lead (p. 19)
DS ≤ NS + (P + U) in the spirit of Greenberg–Madras and Parekh–Gallager; completion times chained fluid → nominal → discrete (p. 18)
flow-shop example: an additive (Jmax − 1)Pmax is necessary for any comparison with the fluid bound (p. 27)
two-machine family showing STT is not asymptotically optimal (12k + 2 against 9k) (p. 39)
experiments: ft10 with N = 1–1000: gap to N·Cmax 491–653 against a bound of about 5,000, relative error 0.88 at N = 1 and below 1% at N = 100 (Table 10, pp. 33–34); 82 OR-library instances, some with zero gap (Table 11, pp. 33–36); eight dispatch rules: STT beats FSA on all ten swv instances at N = 1, FSA is best from N = 10 except on swv01 (Tables 12–16, pp. 37–38); shifting bottleneck better where it finishes, but it fails at N = 10 or 20 on three of four instances (Tables 18–21, pp. 39–41); under five seconds per instance on an Ultra 10 Sun (p. 41).
positioning: Smaller additive error than Sevast'janov's when I is small, and simpler to implement (p. 4); practical where approximation schemes are not (p. 5); generalizes ordering by LP start times to start times computed on the fly (p. 3).
writing: Title in From-X-to-Y form naming the transplant (p. 1); the abstract leads with the guarantee, then the benchmark error rates by N (p. 1).
limits_future: The tightest additive error is open, conjectured (Jmax − 1)Pmax (pp. 27, 41); FSA targets jobs with multiplicity and its error at N = 1 is large (Table 10, p. 34); offered as 'a candidate for practical application' without deployment (p. 41).

method_links.note: duels the incumbent heuristics (eight dispatch rules of similar running time, the shifting bottleneck) and prints where FSA loses; each instance has a gap to a lower bound, but there is no exact solve or certificate beyond that bound
a queueing-control relaxation supplies both the bound and the schedule for a deterministic IO problem

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: asymptotic optimality as the warrant for a simple heuristic
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: an additive error independent of multiplicity makes FSA asymptotically optimal; the experiments show the asymptotic regime already at moderate N

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: policy from the relaxation, certified by the same relaxation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the schedule tracks the fluid optimum and its makespan is measured against the fluid bound Cmax; zero gaps certify optimality
the title 'From fluid relaxations to practical algorithms' names the move from queueing-control relaxations to a scheduling algorithm

transferable: For a combinatorial problem with repeated job types, solve the fluid relaxation in closed form and discretize by scheduling in order of nominal start times that track the fluid schedule and are corrected for precedence; prove an additive error independent of multiplicity (pp. 9–11, 26–27).
Prove that a discrete schedule tracks a continuous one with a potential that charges lag and credits at most one job of lead (p. 19).

Test an asymptotic heuristic across multiplicities N on standard benchmarks, report its error against the lower bound beside the theoretical bound, and report where a slower incumbent wins and where it stops running (pp. 33–41).
Show that incumbent rules are not asymptotically optimal with a small instance family whose makespan stays a constant factor above the congestion bound (p. 39).

quotes.text: the results of this paper imply that as the number of jobs increases, the combinatorial structure of the problem is increasingly less important, and as a result, a fluid approximation of the problem becomes increasingly exact.
Our experiments show that FSA is competitive although slightly worse than the shifting bottleneck heuristic, whenever such a comparison is possible.

title: Joint network pricing and resource allocation
contribution: Formulates joint network pricing and capacity allocation as a priced multi-product newsvendor whose revenue at optimal prices is concave in the allocations for log-concave or lognormal demand noise (an LP after piecewise linearization), proposes three rolling-horizon heuristics including an LP over one-dimensional DP value functions, and bounds the value of dynamic stochastic pricing by demand variability.
problem_entry: {AP+SD} Airline revenue management optimizes seat inventory at given prices, and joint pricing-allocation models are single-leg or single-product; entry: a multi-product, capacity-constrained, priced, multi-period newsvendor for airline pricing (pp. 1–4).
key_idea: Eliminate price per product; R(x) at the optimal price is concave under log-concave or lognormal noise, although revenue is not jointly concave (Theorems 1–2, pp. 6–7); piecewise-linearize to an LP (pp. 7–8); multi-period heuristics DAM, DDM and DPM, the last an LP over one-dimensional DP value functions (pp. 9–12).
assumptions: Production at the start of the period, mean demand depending only on own price, lost sales without salvage (p. 4); assumption 2 admitted necessary for tractability (pp. 4–5); multiplicative demand D = μ(p)Z (p. 5); partitioned inventory control (p. 13); synthetic single-hub airline data, Erlang demand with CV² = 33% (p. 15).
proof_devices: price eliminated per product; concavity of R(x) cited from Zabel and Young (Theorems 1–2, p. 6); lack of joint concavity shown by an example (pp. 6–7)
Normal-noise counterexample to concavity (p. 6)
bound ladder J_LB ≤ J_static ≤ J_dynamic ≤ E[F(z)] ≤ F(E z) via perfect foresight and Jensen's inequality (Theorems 3–7, pp. 13–14)
concave piecewise-linear value functions make DPM's allocation problem an LP rather than a MIP (p. 11)
experiments: 1000 simulated demand runs per policy (p. 16); network-wide pricing gains up to 22% over a decentralized benchmark p∞ (p. 17); DAM ≈ DPM under constant elasticity, DPM clearly better only when elasticity varies (pp. 17–18); the stochastic model beats the deterministic one and the upper bound is not very tight (p. 19); scale factors 1 to 10 have no significant effect (p. 19); table values unreadable in the OCR text.
positioning: Disputes Gallego–van Ryzin (1997) and Paschalidis–Tsitsiklis (2000), attributing their asymptotic optimality of static deterministic pricing to Poisson demand (pp. 4, 14–15, 19); criticizes Weatherford's single-leg joint model as not scaling to networks (p. 2).
writing: Calls the strongest heuristic 'an elegant combination of linear and dynamic programming' in the abstract and the conclusions (pp. 1, 21); states expectations for each heuristic before the experiments and checks them afterwards (pp. 10–12, 18).
limits_future: No real data (p. 15); cross-elasticities, value-function concavity, DPM re-optimizing allocations, and the nested two-stage approach left to further research (pp. 5, 12, 21).

method_links.note: a priced network newsvendor kept in a solver class (concave R(x), then a piecewise-linear LP), with the tractability device stated and its distributional boundary shown by a counterexample
decisions scored by simulated revenue against a naive decentralized pricing rule, but on generated data with no owner or field data

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: single-component DP values as IP coefficients
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: DPM solves one-dimensional DPs per product and uses their piecewise-linear value functions as the objective of the network allocation program (an LP when concave), following an idea from Bertsimas et al. (2001)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: trace a rival's asymptotic result to its distributional assumption
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the bound ladder shows static deterministic pricing approaching optimality only as demand variability vanishes, which scaling achieves under Poisson but not under multiplicative demand; confirmed by the scaling experiment

transferable: When a joint (quantity, price) objective is not jointly concave, optimize price inside each item, prove that the value is concave in quantity, and piecewise-linearize it so the coupling constraints stay an LP (pp. 5–8).
For a network DP, solve one-dimensional DPs per product and use their value functions as piecewise-linear objectives of the allocation LP, re-solved on a rolling horizon (pp. 11–12).
Bracket the optimal dynamic value between a static lower bound and a perfect-foresight upper bound to show which features (demand variance, scale) can change the answer (pp. 13–15).

quotes.text: This simplification was necessary to show that our model has certain desirable properties that allow efficient solution methods.

Since we did not have real data to run numerical experiments, we have written a computer program that automatically generates test problems according to prespecified demand, network and fare settings.

title: An Optimization Approach to Credit Risk
contribution: Uses LP and Farkas duality to bound the survival probabilities and prices of credit-risky bonds from observed bid-ask prices under no-arbitrage alone, and adds robust discount factors, a minimum-perturbation repair of infeasible data and an integer program for rating classification, tested on simulated and July 1999 market data.
problem_entry: {LO+RO+IO; AP} Credit models need default and recovery assumptions that are not always easy to validate; entry: extract information from market prices assuming only no-arbitrage (pp. 2–3).
key_idea: Survival probabilities as LP variables: no arbitrage holds iff a monotone π satisfies bid ≤ q + Aπ ≤ ask (Theorem 1, pp. 6–7); min/max LPs bound π and test-bond prices (Theorem 2, pp. 9–10); robust counterparts handle discount-factor error (pp. 11–14); Freund–Vera repairs infeasibility (pp. 15–16); an IP classifies ratings (pp. 16–17).
assumptions: No-arbitrage with or without transaction costs and a spanning set of traded risky bonds (p. 5); equal default probabilities within a group (p. 5); recovery as a known fraction of notional (pp. 7, 10); simulated Poisson defaults with λ = 0.02 and uniform bid-ask noise (p. 18); real bonds of July 2, 1999 with the Bloomberg Treasury curve (pp. 26–27).
proof_devices: Farkas lemma: infeasibility of the price system yields an explicit arbitrage portfolio (Theorem 1, pp. 6–7)
min/max LPs over the price-consistent set (Theorem 2, pp. 9–10)
LP duality for robust counterparts over polyhedral sets, budget Γ normalized by standard deviations (Theorem 3, pp. 12–14)
Freund–Vera LP for the minimum-norm perturbation that restores feasibility (Theorem 4, pp. 15–16)
binary assignment with the linking constraint |π^i − v^k| ≤ (1 − z_ik)e (p. 17)
experiments: Simulated: bounds tighten with more bonds (five give a 5% range, little gain beyond twenty), maturity mismatch and wider spreads widen them, an apparent recovery effect is traced to the spread generator, robust bounds are tighter than nominal ones, and classification separates λ differences of 0.001 (pp. 18–26); real: the Southwestern Bell test bond lies inside the bounds except for recovery in [0.75, 1], and AA is separated from BBB− but not from AA− (pp. 26–29); seconds per problem (p. 29); no rival credit model run; table numbers unreadable in the OCR text.
positioning: Positions no-arbitrage bounds as a data-driven complement to firm-value and intensity-based models (pp. 2–3, 29); robust LP machinery cited from Ben-Tal–Nemirovski, El Ghaoui et al. and Bertsimas et al. (p. 12).
writing: Contributions listed per section (pp. 3–4); limits stated plainly in the concluding remarks (p. 29).
limits_future: The bounds do not model specific factors (p. 29); adjacent ratings cannot be separated (p. 29); recovery must be known or scanned (p. 10).

method_links.note: a finance question owned by stochastic credit models written as LPs, with structure read off the dual (Farkas certificate = arbitrage)
the Γ budget appears, but robustness narrows the computed bounds instead of pricing conservatism, and no price curve is reported

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: assume only what can be estimated, worst-case the rest
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: only no-arbitrage and observed bid-ask prices are assumed; every survival probability and test price is bounded over all consistent probability vectors
infeasible market data (discount-factor errors) are repaired by the minimum-norm perturbation that restores feasibility instead of deleting bonds

transferable: When a no-arbitrage condition is linear in unknown probabilities, compute the min and max of each unknown over the price-consistent set; the Farkas certificate of infeasibility is the arbitrage trade (pp. 6–10).
Calibrate an unobserved parameter by scanning it and excluding values at which an observed price leaves the computed bounds (p. 10).
Repair infeasible real data with the minimum-norm perturbation that restores feasibility instead of deleting observations (pp. 15–16).
Recheck an apparent parameter effect in synthetic experiments against the way the noise was generated (pp. 21–22).

quotes.text: Our overall objective in this paper is to demonstrate that a lot of information can be extracted from existing market prices assuming only a relatively weak condition: non-existence of arbitrage in credit risky markets.
While the bounds we derive do not model explicitly specific factors, they work directly with the data, and thus are appealing from a practical point of view.

title: Optimal mean-variance bounds on the expectation of the highest order statistics
contribution: April 2004 preprint of S154: the tight upper bound on the expected maximum of random variables with given means and variances is a univariate convex problem solved by bisection and attained by an n-atom extremal distribution, with two closed forms, an SDP under covariances, and bounds for general order statistics.
problem_entry: {CP+AP} Classical order-statistic bounds assume independence or are not tight under general means and variances; entry: compute the tight bound over all distributions with the given moments (pp. 2–3).
key_idea: x_{n:n} ≤ z_{n:n} + Σ(x_i − z_i)^+ gives a convex reformulation (Theorem 1, p. 4); the inner supremum is closed-form (Proposition 1, p. 5); an exchange argument leaves a strictly convex univariate problem solved by bisection (Theorem 2, pp. 5–6, 8); covariances lead to an SDP through the moment dual (pp. 11–12).
assumptions: Only means and variances (optionally covariances), no independence (p. 1); σ_i > 0 for simplicity, relaxed in §2.3 (pp. 4, 10); Q ≻ 0 for the SDP to be exact (p. 11); nonnegative asset prices not modelled (p. 15).
proof_devices: pointwise majorization of the maximum plus univariate worst cases (Theorem 1, Proposition 1, pp. 4–5)
Cauchy–Schwarz for the inner supremum, with a two-point attaining distribution (p. 5)
exchange argument collapsing z to a scalar (pp. 6, 12–13)
n-atom extremal distribution as the tightness certificate (Theorem 3, pp. 6–7)
moment dual and global nonnegativity of a quadratic as an SDP (pp. 11–12)
experiments: Lookback option from Andreasen (n = 10, K = 70–140): at K = 70 the tight bound is 75.38 against Boyle–Lin 327.97, Arnold–Groeneveld 81.20 and Aven 77.79 (Table 2, p. 16); 100 random moment sets with n = 30: closed form (15) errs 7.73% against 22.86% and 16.91% (Table 3, p. 17); second order statistic: (33) errs 1.04% against 3.13% (Table 4, p. 18); Pentium II, under a minute in total, SeDuMi for the SDP (pp. 14, 16).
positioning: Recovers Arnold–Groeneveld's identical-moment bound (pp. 8, 13) and extends Lai–Robbins from known marginals to known moments (p. 6).
writing: Contributions listed by section (p. 3); concedes constructed cases where the closed forms lose to the classical bounds (p. 18).
limits_future: Tight bounds for general k under mean-variance and covariance information left to future research (p. 19); bisection for k < n not guaranteed tight (p. 18).

method_links.note: a probability question written as a convex program; the worst case is read from an extremal distribution and, with covariances, from the dual SDP
the incumbent closed-form bounds are run on a published example and on random moment data; the certificate is tightness through an extremal distribution, not a gap (as on S154's c10 card)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: tight-or-nothing: bounds certified by extremal distributions
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: tightness defined as attainment (Definition 1) and shown by an explicit n-atom distribution and by the identical-moment construction

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Subsume the incumbent as a special case
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: for identical means and variances the bound reproduces Arnold–Groeneveld's exactly; the result extends Lai–Robbins

transferable: For sup E[max_i x_i] under marginal moments, bound the max by z + Σ(x_i − z)^+, take each term's univariate worst case in closed form, and minimize over the scalar z (pp. 4–6).
Turn the endpoints of a bisection bracket into closed-form bounds and compare them, with the classical bounds, against the exact value on random instances (pp. 8–9, 17–18).
Certify tightness by writing down the extremal discrete distribution built from the optimal z (pp. 6–7).

quotes.text: All our results are distribution-free with no explicit assumption of independence made.
While cases can be constructed for which both the bounds are weaker that either of Arnold and Groeneveld and Aven's bounds, the results suggest that the bounds are useful.

title: Robust discrete optimization under ellipsoidal uncertainty sets
contribution: Shows that robust 0–1 optimization with correlated ellipsoidal cost uncertainty is NP-hard for polynomially solvable problems, that uncorrelated identical-variance ellipsoids keep the nominal complexity (n + 1 nominal solves), and gives an ε-approximation and a Frank–Wolfe-type local search with gap bounds for the uncorrelated case, plus a solution-dependent budget model.
problem_entry: {RO+IO} Scenario robustness can make polynomial problems NP-hard while budget sets preserve complexity, and ellipsoidal sets for discrete problems lacked complexity results; entry: does ellipsoidal cost robustness change complexity, and can the problem be solved fast in practice (p. 2)?
key_idea: Correlated ellipsoids embed Kouvelis–Yu's two-scenario problem (Theorem 1, pp. 4–5); for concave f, min c'x + f(d'x) reduces to nominal problems with costs c + η(w)d (Theorem 2, pp. 5–6); a piecewise-linear approximation and a Frank–Wolfe-type local search handle general d (pp. 7–16); Γ = f(e'x) generalizes the budget model (pp. 16–18).
assumptions: X ⊆ {0,1}^n accessed through a nominal linear-optimization oracle (pp. 3, 9); uncertainty in the objective only (p. 3); diagonal covariance for the algorithms (p. 5); independent symmetric costs for the budget model's probability bound (p. 16).
proof_devices: reduction from the NP-hard two-scenario robust problem by writing max{a, b} = (a + b)/2 + |a − b|/2 as a rank-one ellipsoid (Theorem 1, pp. 4–5)
subgradient linearization of a concave function over the finite range of d'x (Theorem 2, pp. 5–6)
breakpoints placed for a given maximum approximation error (Proposition 3, pp. 8–9)
improvement, monotonicity and local optimality of the linearized local search, and a gap bound from two local optima (Theorems 5–6, pp. 11–16)
duality of the inner maximization for the solution-dependent budget model (Theorem 8, pp. 16–18)
experiments: Robust knapsack, |N| = 200, b = 20,000, Ω = 1–5: optimum reached in few iterations, very small gap where two local minima arise (Table 2, p. 20); uniform matroid, |N| = 200–20,000, Ω = 1–3, 100 instances each: mostly optimal within fewer than 10 nominal solves, iterations barely growing with |N| (Table 3, pp. 21–22); no exact baseline run; table numbers unreadable in the OCR text.
positioning: Extends Bertsimas–Sim budgeted robust discrete optimization to ellipsoidal sets and contrasts it with Kouvelis–Yu (pp. 2–4); links the problem to parametric discrete optimization (pp. 6–7).
writing: Frames the question as 'the price (in increased complexity) of robustness' and calls the first result unfortunately negative (p. 4).
limits_future: Complexity under a diagonal covariance left open (p. 21); Algorithm 1 is not polynomial in bit size (p. 10); the generalized budget model costs more computation (p. 18).

method_links.note: class preservation tested and its boundary printed: budget sets and identical-variance ellipsoids keep the nominal class (n + 1 nominal solves), correlated ellipsoids do not (NP-hard)
the price of robustness measured in complexity rather than in objective value; Γ made solution-dependent to reduce conservatism

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: robust = nominal on modified data (structure inheritance)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the robust problem with concave f(d'x) equals the best of nominal problems with modified costs c + η(w)d, n + 1 of them for identical variances

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: two-sided local search brackets the optimum with a computable gap
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the linearized local search run from both ends of the subgradient range yields two local optima whose disagreement bounds the gap, closed by bisecting the range

transferable: To show that a robust version is hard, rewrite a known hard robust problem as a special case of your uncertainty set through an algebraic identity (pp. 4–5).
For min c'x + f(d'x) with f concave over 0–1 sets, enumerate the attainable values of d'x and solve the nominal problem with costs c + f'(w)d; few values preserve complexity (pp. 5–6).
Run a local search from both ends of the subgradient range; differing local optima give a certified gap that bisection closes (pp. 13–16, 19).

quotes.text: Our first result is unfortunately negative. Under ellipsoidal uncertainty sets with general covariance matrices, the price of robustness is an increase in computational complexity.
A message of the present paper is that the complexity of robust discrete optimization is affected by the choice of the uncertainty set.
